text.title: W3C Design Tokens Standard Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules on the DTCG format itself: `$value`/`$type` and type inheritance, reserved `$` and forbidden name characters, alias resolution, draft-revision pinning, composite token structure, and file identity. Each is checkable by opening the `.tokens.json` file.

rule.statement: Every token object MUST have `$value`, and MUST resolve a `$type` either on itself or on the nearest ancestor group that declares one. A token whose type cannot be resolved by walking up the group chain is invalid.

rationale.source: W3C Design Tokens Community Group format spec — Design token / Type

rule.rationale: Type is what every downstream transform keys on: it decides whether a value becomes `UIColor`, a Compose `Color`, or a CSS `oklch()` string. An untyped token falls through the transform table and is emitted as a raw string, so the platform build succeeds and ships a literal `{...}` or an unconverted hex into a place that cannot render it.

rule.statement: Group and token names MUST NOT begin with `$`, and MUST NOT contain `{`, `}` or `.`. Any object key starting with `$` that is not a spec-defined property (`$value`, `$type`, `$description`, `$extensions`, `$deprecated`) is invalid.

rationale.source: DTCG format spec — Groups / Character restrictions

rule.rationale: `$` is the namespace the spec reserves for its own properties, so a group named `$brand` is indistinguishable from a format key and a strict parser either drops it or errors. `.` is the alias path delimiter, so a token literally named `color.brand` can never be referenced — `{color.brand}` resolves as a two-level path into a group that does not exist.

rule.statement: References MUST use the full-string brace form `"{group.subgroup.token}"` as the entire `$value`, MUST terminate at a token (never a group), MUST NOT form a cycle, and the resolved `$type` MUST match the referencing token's type.
rule.rationale: A group has no `$value`, so a reference to one resolves to `undefined`. Most tooling does not fail on that: it writes the unresolved literal `{color.brand}` into the output, producing a CSS declaration the browser discards as invalid at parse time — no build error, no console warning, just the property silently missing.

rule.statement: The artefact MUST record which DTCG draft revision (date or commit) it targets, and the validator/transform toolchain MUST be pinned to a version that implements that revision.

rationale.source: DTCG format spec status — Community Group draft, not a W3C Recommendation

rule.rationale: The `$value` shape for `color` and `dimension` changed across drafts — from plain strings (`"#ff0000"`, `"16px"`) to structured objects (`colorSpace`/`components`/`alpha`; `{ value, unit }`). A parser built for one revision rejects or silently mis-reads the other, and because both forms are valid JSON the error surfaces deep inside the platform build rather than at validation.

rule.statement: Composite types (`typography`, `border`, `shadow`, `transition`, `gradient`, `strokeStyle`) MUST express `$value` as an object of named sub-values, each itself a valid token value or an alias. CSS shorthand strings such as `"1px solid #000"` or `"600 16px/1.5 Inter"` are rejected.
rule.rationale: A shorthand is a CSS-specific serialisation, and it collapses exactly the structure the format exists to preserve. Android needs the width in dp and the colour as a packed int; iOS needs a `CGFloat` and a `UIColor`. Neither can be derived without re-parsing a string whose grammar the transform does not own, so shorthand composites are either dropped or hand-duplicated per platform — which is the drift tokens were adopted to remove.

rule.statement: Token files MUST use the `.tokens` or `.tokens.json` extension (media type `application/design-tokens+json`), and all vendor-specific data MUST live under `$extensions` keyed in reverse-domain form (`com.figma.*`, `net.faion.*`). Vendor keys placed directly on a token object are rejected.
rule.rationale: Tooling discovers token files by extension, so a `theme.json` is simply not picked up by the pipeline that was pointed at the directory. Un-namespaced vendor keys are worse: they occupy the same key space the spec may later define, so a strict parser drops them today and a future revision may reinterpret them, in both cases without an error.

rule.statement: Do NOT apply when (a) exactly one platform consumes the tokens and there is no design-tool round-trip — plain CSS custom properties in one file are cheaper and lose nothing; (b) the transform tool in use has no DTCG support, in which case document its native schema rather than authoring a format nothing in the pipeline reads; (c) no build step consumes the file at all and the "tokens" are hand-copied into stylesheets.
rule.rationale: The DTCG format's value is interchange — one authored source feeding multiple platform transforms and a design tool. With a single consumer and no transform, the format adds a JSON layer plus a build step in front of the only file anyone edits, and the JSON drifts from the stylesheet as soon as one hotfix skips it.
